strengths: Conceptual clarity and unification: The paper provides a compelling perspective connecting subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) and SPRING to randomized regularized Kaczmarz and accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) methods from randomized numerical linear algebra.

Resolves a key puzzle in scientific machine learning optimization: Explains why estimating both the stochastic gradient and the Fisher preconditioner using the same mini-batch yields stable, fast convergence rather than destructive noise correlations.

Novel extension to non-least-squares objectives: The formulation of linear least-quadratics (LLQ) and the analysis of SNGD under strong consistency (Theorem 4) extends beyond standard least-squares settings to capture problems like Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) for quantum wavefunctions.

Theoretical explanation for practical heuristics: Proposition 3 provides a clear mathematical explanation for why positive Tikhonov damping (lambda > 0) is necessary when training neural network wavefunctions with subsampled natural gradient methods, showing that non-symmetric projected operators can otherwise have eigenvalues with negative real parts leading to divergence.
High presentation quality: The manuscript is well-written, clearly organized, and thoroughly supported by detailed proofs and illustrative numerical simulations.
weaknesses: Reliance on idealized assumptions: The analysis requires exact consistency (interpolation) and the strong containment condition range(HJ) subset of range(J), as well as an alignment condition (P and J^T J sharing an eigenbasis) in Theorem 4, which strictly hold only in asymptotic or specialized sampling regimes.

Theoretical results for SPRING in LLQ are incomplete: While SNGD is analyzed for LLQ, the accelerated rate for SPRING on LLQ is left as an open conjecture (Conjecture 7), accompanied only by extreme-case verifications and numerical experiments.

Direct importation of LLS rates: For the linear least-squares setting, once the algebraic equivalence between SNGD/SPRING and regularized Kaczmarz/ARK is established, the convergence rates follow directly from existing literature (Goldshlager et al., 2025; Dereziński et al., 2025).

strengths: Unifying perspective via randomized linear algebra: The paper builds an elegant bridge between subsampled natural gradient algorithms (SNGD, SPRING) widely used in scientific machine learning (PINNs and VMC) and the randomized/accelerated Kaczmarz literature (Goldshlager et al., 2025; Dereziński et al., 2025). This conceptually clarifies why joint subsampling of the gradient and Fisher preconditioner is mathematically well-behaved rather than pathological.

First theoretical guarantee for SPRING: By proving an exact iterate-level equivalence between SPRING and the Accelerated Regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method in the linear least-squares setting (Theorem 1), the paper provides the first formal convergence guarantee and acceleration proof for SPRING.

Analysis of non-least-squares setting (LLQ): The formulation of the Linear Least-Quadratics (LLQ) problem directly captures the variational Monte Carlo setup. Proposition 3 provides valuable insight into why a positive regularization parameter $\lambda > 0$ is strictly necessary when subsampling under an anisotropic metric, preventing divergence caused by non-Hermitian step matrices.

Well-structured presentation: The paper is clearly written, thoughtfully positioned in the context of recent scientific ML literature, and transparent about which results derive directly from prior work versus new extensions.
weaknesses: Highly restrictive assumptions for the LLQ setting: The analytical results for LLQ rely on strong idealizations: (i) Assumption 2 requires $\operatorname{range}(HJ) \subseteq \operatorname{range}(J)$, which almost never holds in the overparameterized/subsampled setting unless $J$ spans an invariant subspace of $H$; and (ii) Theorem 4 requires that the expected projection $\bar{P}$ commutes with $J^\top J$, which strictly holds only for specific determinantal point processes or asymptotic Gaussian designs.

Incremental theoretical novelty in the LLS setting: For linear least-squares (Section 3), while the algebraic equivalence between SNGD/SPRING and regularized Kaczmarz/ARK is neat, the convergence rates themselves follow directly from existing analyses in Goldshlager et al. (2025) and Dereziński et al. (2024; 2025).

SPRING on LLQ remains unproven: A primary motivation of the work is explaining the empirical acceleration of SPRING in scientific ML, yet the convergence of SPRING for general LLQ is only stated as a conjecture (Conjecture 7) supported by empirical simulations.

Idealized model problem: The analysis is restricted strictly to linear parametric models $v_\theta = J\theta$ and consistent/interpolating objectives. While reasonable as a local/tangent space proxy, the paper does not analyze the impact of curvature changes or nonlinear parameterizations typical of neural network wavefunctions.

strengths: Important conceptual connection: The paper establishes an elegant and principled equivalence between subsampled natural gradient methods (SNGD and SPRING) popular in scientific machine learning and randomized linear algebra methods (specifically regularized Kaczmarz and Accelerated Regularized Kaczmarz, ARK).

Novel theoretical convergence guarantees: Provides the first fast linear convergence rate for SNGD on consistent linear least-squares (LLS) and general linear least-quadratics (LLQ), as well as the first convergence proof demonstrating the accelerated rate of SPRING over SNGD for LLS.

Theoretical explanation of empirical SciML phenomena: The analysis explains why SNGD can vastly outperform mini-batch SGD on problems with decaying singular values (such as PINNs), why momentum in SPRING delivers up to a square-root acceleration, and why damping/regularization (lambda > 0) is fundamentally required when the function-space Hessian H is anisotropic (Proposition 3).

Clear, structured writing and high mathematical elegance: The manuscript is well organized, motivating the model problems LLQ and LLS directly from quantum VMC and PINN formulations, and the mathematical derivations in the appendices are rigorous and clean.
weaknesses: Restrictive theoretical assumptions for LLQ: Strong consistency requires range(HJ) to be a subset of range(J), meaning the tangent space of the model is an invariant subspace of H, which rarely holds strictly in realistic neural network wavefunctions. Furthermore, Theorem 4 requires that the expected projection matrix shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, which holds strictly only under idealized conditions (e.g., asymptotic Gaussian data or DPP sampling).

Theoretical gap for SPRING on LLQ: While the authors analyze extreme cases (Proposition 6) and conduct numerical experiments, the convergence and acceleration rate of SPRING on general LLQ remains a conjecture (Conjecture 7).

Evaluation restricted to synthetic problems: The empirical validation is entirely on synthetic Gaussian quadratic problems with small dimensions (n=100). Validating the key theoretical insights (such as the divergence condition when lambda is small or the convergence speedup over SGD) on small-scale real PINN or VMC benchmarks would substantially enhance the practical impact.

Minor mathematical presentation typos: In the proof of Proposition 3 (page 15), the text erroneously states 'If xi(lambda) > 0 and M thus has an eigenvalue with negative real part', which should be 'xi(lambda) < 0'. Additionally, in the proof of Corollary 5 (page 17), the bound on alpha states Omega(k^beta kappa_dem^{-1}(J)) instead of kappa_dem^{-2}(J).

strengths: Original and insightful perspective: The paper successfully reframes subsampled natural gradient (SNG) through the lens of sketch-and-project (randomized block Kaczmarz) methods, moving away from the conventional, often inadequate stochastic preconditioning framework.

Resolves the gradient-preconditioner decoupling problem: Previous theoretical analyses commonly decoupled the stochastic gradient and preconditioner using two independent mini-batches, which completely breaks down when the batch size $k \ll n$. By utilizing squared volume sampling (SVS) as a theoretical proxy, the authors prove an exact expectation formula (Lemma 4.1) where the expected direction is a preconditioned gradient step without artificial decoupling.

Rigorous convergence rate analysis: For linear least-quadratics (LLQ), Theorem 5.1 establishes an explicit linear convergence rate governed by $\alpha/\gamma$. This cleanly explains why SNG can exploit spectral decay in the model Jacobian to achieve superlinear scaling in mini-batch size, a phenomenon observed in scientific ML (PINNs, NNWs) that SGD cannot achieve.

Demystifying SPRING: Theorem 6.1 proves an exact algebraic equivalence between the heuristic structured momentum method SPRING and accelerated regularized sketch-and-project, providing a solid theoretical grounding for this popular algorithm.

Clear presentation and honest discussion of limitations: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, carefully positioned within the literature, and transparent about what is proven versus conjectured (e.g., Conjecture 6.2, open questions regarding $\gamma$).
weaknesses: SVS is a theoretical device rather than a practical algorithm: As acknowledged by the authors, SVS is computationally prohibitive for large-scale practical problems. While the paper provides empirical evidence that SVS and uniform sampling behave similarly, a formal theoretical bridge bounding the discrepancy between uniform sampling and SVS for general $k$ remains an open challenge.

Preliminary characterization of the second-moment constant $\gamma$: Proposition 5.3 only provides bounds for extreme cases ($k=1, m$ for $\lambda=0$) or a loose bound under uniform sampling. A full theoretical characterization of $\gamma$ across general intermediate sample sizes $1 < k < m$ under SVS is left open.

Restriction to linear least-quadratics (LLQ): The quantitative convergence rates in Section 5 apply to the linearized/quadratic setting. While standard and well-justified for local convergence in consistent scientific ML problems, full non-asymptotic non-linear convergence guarantees are not established.

Conjecture for accelerated LLQ: The convergence rate for SPRING in the LLQ setting (Conjecture 6.2) is supported by empirical evidence and analogy rather than a rigorous proof, due to the non-trivial interplay between function space curvature $H$ and Nesterov acceleration.

strengths: Conceptual novelty: The paper departs from the conventional and unrealistic two-independent-minibatch decoupling proxy used in prior stochastic natural gradient literature, re-framing subsampled natural gradient descent (SNG) as a sketch-and-project (regularized randomized block Kaczmarz) method.

Theoretical elegance: By introducing squared volume sampling (SVS) as an analytical tool, Lemma 4.1 achieves an exact expectation formula for coupled gradient and preconditioner updates (E[J_S^{+(λ)} r_S] = W~ J^T r). This provides an elegant mechanism to establish global convergence (Theorem 4.2) and explicit linear convergence rates for linear least-quadratics (Theorem 5.1).

Explanation of empirical phenomena: The framework cleanly explains why SNG can achieve superlinear speedup with respect to batch size when the Jacobian exhibits spectral decay (via the sketch-and-project rate α), contrasting sharply with standard SGD limits.

Principled explanation of SPRING: Theorem 6.1 establishes an exact equivalence between the empirical SPRING momentum algorithm and accelerated regularized sketch-and-project methods, demystifying a popular optimizer in scientific machine learning.

Clear presentation and honest discussion: The manuscript is exceptionally well written, clearly structured, and provides transparent discussions of technical limitations, including the role and bounds of the second-moment parameter γ.
weaknesses: Gap between SVS theory and practical uniform sampling: While numerical experiments (Figures 2 and 6) show that SVS-SNG behaves remarkably similarly to uniform sampling, SVS is computationally intractable for practical large-scale training, leaving a theoretical gap between the analyzed SVS proxy and the uniform mini-batching used in real-world applications.

Incomplete theoretical characterization of γ: In the convergence rate scaling α/γ (Theorem 5.1), the quantity γ is only partially characterized (Proposition 5.3 covers edge cases k=1, k=m, or loose bounds under uniform sampling), though the authors acknowledge this openly.

Conjectural status of accelerated LLQ convergence: While Theorem 6.1 establishes the algebraic equivalence of SPRING to accelerated sketch-and-project, the convergence rate for SPRING in the linear least-quadratics setting remains a conjecture (Conjecture 6.2), verified empirically rather than proven mathematically.

Focus on linearized / consistent models: The detailed convergence rate analysis focuses on the linear least-quadratics (LLQ) setting. While well motivated by high-precision scientific machine learning (PINNs/NNWs near consistency), it does not capture the full non-convex and non-linear dynamics of deep network training away from the solution.

strengths: Novel and insightful conceptual framework: By framing subsampled natural gradient (SNG) through the lens of sketch-and-project / randomized block Kaczmarz methods rather than stochastic preconditioning, the paper overcomes the longstanding theoretical limitation of requiring two independent mini-batches to decouple the stochastic gradient and preconditioner.

Mathematical elegance of Lemma 4.1: The derivation showing that under squared volume sampling (SVS), the expected update direction equals a preconditioned gradient step without decoupling (even in small-sample regimes where k << n) is a clean and powerful technical result.

Theoretical explanation for empirical behavior: Theorem 5.1 connects the convergence rate in the linear least-quadratics (LLQ) setting directly to the sketch-and-project rate constant alpha, providing a principled explanation for why SNG can achieve superlinear speedups with sample size when the model Jacobian exhibits fast spectral decay (a known property in scientific ML models).

Demystifying the SPRING algorithm: Theorem 6.1 establishes an exact algebraic equivalence between the heuristic structured-momentum SPRING optimizer and accelerated regularized sketch-and-project methods, giving a solid foundation to an optimizer that previously lacked theoretical justification.

Clear presentation and transparent treatment of limitations: The manuscript is well structured, contextualizes related work thoroughly, clearly distinguishes between proved theorems and conjectures (e.g., Conjecture 6.2), and provides clean proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: Practicality gap of Squared Volume Sampling (SVS): As the authors acknowledge, SVS is computationally intensive and not directly implementable for high-dimensional neural network training. While the authors use it as an analytical proxy and show empirically that it mirrors uniform mini-batching better than the two-batch proxy, the theoretical convergence results do not strictly hold for uniform sampling without further assumptions.

Incomplete analytical characterization of gamma: The quantity gamma (relating to the second moment of the sketch-and-project step) plays a central role in the maximum stable step size and convergence rate (alpha / gamma). However, closed-form or tight upper bounds for gamma under SVS for general intermediate mini-batch sizes (1 < k < m) are left unresolved, with only special cases (k = 1, k = m) or uniform sampling bounds established.

Scope limited to the Linear Least-Quadratics (LLQ) model: The explicit linear convergence rate (Theorem 5.1) is proven only for consistent LLQ problems. While this models local behavior near consistent minima, extending detailed convergence rates to nonlinear and non-convex neural network regimes remains an open challenge.

Conjecture 6.2 is unproven: While the equivalence of SPRING to accelerated sketch-and-project is proven in Theorem 6.1, the resulting convergence rate in the LLQ setting (Conjecture 6.2) is left as a conjecture supported only by numerical experiments.
